Because you are a freelancer, you are considered a sole proprietor. You can deduct business expenses directly from your $8,900 freelance income, which lowers both your income tax and self-employment tax.
*   **Work Supplies ($650):** Fully deductible as a business expense on **Schedule C**.
*   **Home Office Deduction:** You can deduct this against your freelance income, provided the space is used *exclusively and regularly* for your graphic design business. You have two ways to calculate this:
    *   **Simplified Method:** $5 per square foot. (100 sq ft × $5 = **$500 deduction**).
    *   **Actual Expenses Method:** You calculate the percentage of your home used for business (100 sq ft / 850 sq ft = **11.76%**). You can deduct 11.76% of your annual rent ($25,200 × 11.76% = **~$2,963**), plus 11.76% of utilities, renter's insurance, and internet. This method yields a much higher deduction but requires filing **Form 8829**.

### 3. "Above-the-Line" Deductions (Adjustments to Income)
These deductions lower your Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) and can be taken *even if you take the standard deduction*.
*   **Student Loan Interest:** The IRS caps this deduction at **$2,500** per year. Even though you paid $2,700, you can deduct the maximum $2,500. You will receive Form 1098-E from MOHELA, and you will report this on **Schedule 1**.
*   **Self-Employment Tax Deduction:** You get to deduct 50% of the self-employment taxes you pay on your freelance profit. This is calculated on **Schedule SE** and reported on **Schedule 1**.

### 4. Standard vs. Itemized Deductions
*   **Standard Deduction:** For a single filer in 2024, the standard deduction is **$14,600**.
*   **Itemized Deductions:** If you itemized, you could deduct your $800 charitable donation to Doctors Without Borders, plus your state income taxes (capped at $10,000). 
*   **The Verdict:** Your total itemized deductions ($800 + state taxes) would be well under $14,600. Therefore, taking the **Standard Deduction** is almost certainly the better choice for you. *(Note: Business expenses and student loan interest are handled separately, so you still get those benefits while taking the standard deduction!)*
